messages.subject: Sample size calculation
parts:
Dear blavann users and bayesians,
I am struggling with the concept of a-priori sample size calculation in Bayesian analysis. I found some articles in Google but they confounded me even more because they point to Monte Carlo Simulation, the same technique that is used in the frequentist approach for the a-priori calculation of sample size in structural equation modeling.

Given this, I would like to know what is the theory and the practice of a-priori sample size calculation in Bayesian SEM. Please refer me to some illustrative documents and let me know if there are R packages or some other software that can be easily used for the Bayesian calculation of sample size in parameter estimation. 

Thank you very much in advance for any advice.

Sincerely,
Mauro

messages.author: 5d4f9e7f97c21008
messages.subject: Re: Sample size calculation
parts:
Hi Mauro,

The recommendations for Monte Carlo simulations for sample size determination are a good start. For sample size determination you need to first define a criteria of interest. In frequentist analyses the criteria is often p < .05, but in either frequentist or Bayesian analyses you can use other criteria as well (e.g. the width of an interval estimate, if an interval estimate contains a value, a specific Bayes factor). Then with a Monte Carlo simulation you define your population values, simulate data, analyze the data and determine the proportion of replications which meet your criteria, you would then repeat the simulation, varying sample sizes until the proportion of replications meets your desired level (e.g. .8 or .9). 

Most of my work on this issue has been with frequentist analyses but the same ideas apply with Bayes. The hardest thing to do with Bayes is to determine the criteria of interest (which will depend on the research question you're interested in). I don't have any references specifically for Bayesian SEM, but John Kruschke's BEST approach illustrates the same technique for simpler models (http://www.indiana.edu/~kruschke/BEST/), but if you're interested in software, there's not (currently) a one stop shop. I think you could do this by generating data for each replication (e.g. with the simsem package) and then analyzing the results with blavaan, using a loop or apply statement (I think you might even be able to trick simsem into running blavaan with a bit of coding).

Alex
